blocks.x: I mentioned we're interviewing Mr. Isaiah Robinson. This is Bill Russell, and Ralph Collins is also here. And the place is 821 North Claiborne, is that right? That's right. And the date is April 29th, I believe, 28th maybe. 28th. 28th, 1961. Do you mind giving your full name? Do you have any middle initials?
No middle name at all. Isaiah Robinson, that's all.
I guess most people have called you Ike Robinson. I've heard some of them talk about Big Ike because you're rather tall.
Yeah.
Can you tell us just where you were born and when it was, your birth date?
I was born in Lafourche, Paris, March the 16th, 1891.
Yeah.
Where is that? That's up the river, is it? Or west of here? Yeah. West. Up the S.P. What town is that near? Thibodeau. Oh, Thibodeau.
Yeah.
Can you tell us about the earliest music you heard up there? Were there any bands up there when you were a boy?

Well, a band by the name of Joe Gabriel. Oh, yes. I heard people talking to him. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And I used to play in the, see Joe Gabriel was number one, three were number one. And I was playing, I played in number two.
And the number one and number two band?
Yeah. I had a number one, Joe Gabriel was number one.
He was in the number one band?
No, I was in the number two band.
I see.
Yeah.
But he was in the number one band.
Yeah.
Just a minute. I'll point this microphone, this, all the big trucks have figured out what that hum is now.
You can set the door if you want.
That's all right. No.
Well, maybe we better a little bit. Just see if it won't be too warm for you.
No, it ain't going to be too warm for me. As far as we don't set that far. Because all those trucks make sort of a hum going.
That's what I said. The windows open anyway.

Red Becker was talking the other day. He came over here and said there's such a much truck noise all night. He said he didn't think anybody could sleep on this street. I guess you get used to it. Oh, yeah. I've been here 26 years. I've been getting used to it. It doesn't bother me. There used to be where there's a lot of cars going by now. But Jack's blue. He didn't bother. Excuse the interruption. That'll pick it up better now.
You're saying there were two bands. Yeah. Did they have any? Were they brass bands? No, orchestra. Orchestra? Yeah. Did they have, what were they called? String bands?
Yeah. See, that consisted with trombone, drum, cornet, clarinet, violin, and bass.
I see.
That was the same in both of the bands.
Yeah. Both of us had the same.
I remember Lewis James told us he was raised up there.
Yeah.
And he knew some of the Gabriels too.
Yeah. Well, he used to play with Gabriels.
He played.
Yeah.
Is that the same family that August Lenois is married to? His wife's name is Gabriel, I believe.
August. Which August?
He's from Timothee? Bass player. We talked to him last week. Let's see. Was one of the clarinet player, one of the Gabriels? What did this?
The Gabriels was the violin player.
He was the violin player, the leader of your band.
No, no, no. He wasn't the leader of my band.
Of the number one band.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, his...
Who else was in your band?
Who else? My band was... My band was... We... Consist of a fellow by the name of Shield Table... Let's see... Shield guy. He used to play trombone.
Well, what instrument did you start in?
I started a guitar. That's what I'm coming up to. I started a guitar. That's when I was in the country.
Yeah.

With a shield table, trombone, a fellow by the name of Bud Green. He was on drums. Joe Banks was on cornet. Little Willie, well, he was playing clarinet in our band at them times. And I was guitar. And a little fellow by the name of Alfred Dixon. He was playing bass.
Yeah. Yeah.
We didn't have no violin in our...
Before I forget it, did your father, mother, anyone in your family play music before you?
No.
Did you have any brothers or older brothers or sisters? Anyone that played music?
None of them played music. I'm the only one.
The only one?
Yeah.
Excuse the introduction. Go ahead and tell about your band if there's anything else you can tell about the type of music they played. They played for dances.
Yeah. That's what I was dancing.
And you remember who was in Joe Gabriel's band, the other band?
Yeah. stuff
He still plays a little bit, I think.
Yeah. Joe Gabriel, he was the violin player. And Nettie James, that was the guitar player. The fellow that played bass, he called him bourgeois.
What did you say? You used to call those James? What's his nickname? Dodoos. Dodoos?
Yeah. How did you get that name out of it? I don't know, that's what we used to call it. I never knew that. One of the way I left out was Pallet. His name was Henry James.
What did he play?
He used to play bass, he used to play clarinet. Then when Titin died, he started playing trombone.
Did you have any teacher on the guitar when you started?
Just picked that up.
Just picked it up.
Yeah.
Have you heard many other players besides the Gabriel band? Were there any other bands around or other musicians that you heard when you were a kid up there?
Yeah. Yeah. They had a, what's this great band up in Donisonville? Claiborne.
Oh yeah, Claiborne Williams.

Yeah. I believe you heard them. Yeah. Yeah. They had a band band. They had a little band in Napoleonville. I knew a couple of the fellas. Trombone played by the name of Lewis Hines. Cornet player by the name of, God, it's been so long though. Really that thing kind of slipped me up.
Yeah. Anyway, there was a band there in Napoleonville, a record.
Yeah. A record dance band. That's right.
Where did you play in those times? Did you play in Thibodeau or just around the country?
No, in Thibodeau and we used to go around all of them down the bayou. Sometimes we'd go west. Yeah. Around Donau, Chakarula, Buey, all them places.
How, how, in your department going there? What bayou is that on? The Tash or the, uh?
No, Barle Fush.
Oh, oh, that's right.
Yeah. I was gonna say, how did you travel in those days? Did you travel on the water or on the roads?
No, we used to travel in, uh, truck and train.
Well, when you traveled by truck, was that a motor truck in those days?
Yeah, a motor truck.
About when would that be? Do you remember about how old you'd be?
How old were you when you started in music? I forgot that.
Let's see, I started playing, uh, we could share about 1914. I was playing with James. I was playing with James. I was playing with James. You played in the band?
Yeah, I was playing with James.
I used to play guitar, you know, all around. Yeah. That was before that, but around 1914 or 16, I started playing in the band.
Did you ever have any brass bands up in the country or parades that you can remember?
Yeah, I used to have a band in Tippit Oval. Call it, uh, Eureka Brass Band.
Or, same as, Eureka, same name as they had here then?
Yeah. No, Eureka, that's right, the Eureka Brass Band. We had about the best band out on the bayou. Did you play in it later then?
No, I didn't play in it.
You didn't play in it?
Yeah.
What was that name again?
Eureka Brass Band. Eureka? Yeah. Uh-huh. Something like Eureka, I believe it's Eureka Brass Band.
It's a little different name.
Yeah.
Um, how big a band was it about?
Oh, it was about 12, 14 pieces. Pretty big band then.
Yeah.
Then you, he came down here one, uh, I think it was the old fellas then, he won the prize.
Well, you did, I never played. Were you playing in that band? No, I didn't play in it. So you never did play in it?
No, I never did play in it. In fact, I was, I was small. Oh, yeah.

Did they have many parades up there on the holidays? Or what did they have parades for? Like, I didn't hear they have them on Sunday, almost every Sunday, you know, in the summer. Yeah, I know, I know that. Did they have them very often up there?

Sometimes they have a parade, uh, like the old fellas turn out like that, well, they have a little parade. For the different organizations then? Yeah. See, and them times, uh, they used to play for that carnival in Tebido.
Well, they have, do they have a pretty big, uh, celebration up there for carnival too?
Yeah, they have, they have about five or six floats. They do? Mm-hmm. Used to have two bands. Yeah. They had Tebido and the band from Donner from there.
Oh, yeah.
Mm-hmm. When did you take up trombone? I'd taken up trombone and, uh, just after the First World War.
That's around about 1918. Mm-hmm. Were you still living up there in Tebido then? No, I was living in Tebido. I was living in Tebido. I didn't come down here until 1921.

Did you have a teacher on trombone? When I came here I had a teacher. Mm-hmm. About seventh That's around about 1918. Were you still living up there in Thibodeau then? No, we're living in Thibodeau. I didn't come down here until 1921. Did you have a teacher on trombone? When I came here I had a teacher. A fella used to live up on 6th Street, you should call him Professor Perkins. Oh yeah, Dave Perkins. I've heard of him. Never doing that. Yeah, taking lessons from him.
What made you pick up the trombone there in Thibodeau?
We run out of the trombone player. He moved down here. So he gave me the trombone.
Is that in the Gabriel Band, the number 2 band? No. Is that in the number 2 Gabriel Band? Number 2 Band. That's right.
Was that his trombone you were using? Did you get one of them?
No. You see how in them times they buy. The band used to buy all this.
They owned their own band on the instruments.
Yeah, that's right. If you quit you had to leave it there.
I see. Do you remember what make it was?
Let's see. Was that a corn or what?
What kind of a horn did you like when you got one of your own? What kind did you use? I used to like to eat corn. A lot of people do. Yeah. I know some people think the Holton is a good trombone too.
I'd have a little bit spooly for them. What would you do? I wish corn or a marten.
That's a good make I know. Yeah.
Yeah, that was my trombone. He eat corn or he's a marten. My last one was a marten.
Jim Robinson has a marten now. Yeah. His new horn is a marten.
A marten now.
It's a good.
Yeah, nice. But I think C.E. Con got a better trombone than they never. To me, to my days, they used to I know. Like it was a more keener tone than the trombone.
Well, when you took up trombone first to play up in Thibodeau, did you have any help at all? You say you didn't have any lessons or teachers?
No, we just used to just battle it out ourselves. Just figure it out. Yeah.
Do you think that's a pretty good way to first start on the instrument?
No, I think you should have with the teacher. You think you should have?
Yeah.
That's the best way. Start with the teacher. Start right.
Well, how long before you could play in the band then with them in the orchestra or whatever it was? Did it take you a year or so to learn it or just a few weeks?

No, a couple of weeks. When you started. Yeah. Yeah. Cause we was hard up for, for me. You needed somebody to earn. You needed somebody there to fill in. Sure. So I, they start to fill in. You learn me, I start vaping, vaping, vaping. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Finally, I kind of got it pretty good and, uh, the fella down on the car that he was pretty fair reader. He taught me. Was that Banks? Yeah.
Me and him so, we, we had to work hard, dude.

Rehearsal every, every night anyway. Cause I was working in the day. You do a lot of rehearsing then? Yeah. So, finally around a couple of months I could make out. Yeah. That's the only name you had for the bands is number one and number two. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Did they have any halls up there? Dance halls? Oh yeah. Clubhouses? Or did you play mostly? We used to play in halls.
Yeah. Thibodeaux had a place they called, uh, it was the fire ground. Oh. It's torn down now. They had a pavilion now.
Yeah, open on the floor, all around on the side. Get cold, you just set the windows down. I had another place up there, but this open alley, you could call it Cox.
Like a picnic ground? They had picnics and all there?
Yeah, Coxwood. They had plenty of trees. He had a pavilion out there for the dance room, but it was open now.
Are those mostly colored or white, those picnics and things?

In Cox, that's strictly white. I want to say colored. Yeah, it's colored. Yeah, I want to say colored. And the flagrown was colored. Well, the white pavilion, they had that round up, I think, they call that Second Street. No. Well, that was for the white.

I've never been in Thibodeau except to ride through. I don't know much about the town. Well, it doesn't change around something. Nice little place now, you tell me. How big, how many people there? A few thousand or a couple of thousand? How big was it those days? You know?
I never been noticing. That's about a year. It must have been about 7,000 or 8,000 people.
Fairly big town, man. Yeah, it's pretty big enough. Yeah. Everything keeps growing. Yeah.
You got streets out there out of Newinor. Yeah. I've been waiting there a good while.
Did you have, you said you had a day job too, you'd work in the daytime too?
Yeah, I used to work on the railroad.
That'd be the SB, was that?
Southern Pacific. I'd wait there long enough that I had an annual pass. Oh, cool. Yeah, I started waking on the railroad when I was about 17 years old.
Yeah.
I'd wait down there until I came down here in 21. I'm 21.
I was gonna ask you, when you were making out on your trombone, did you never play, you never played a parade with it then, did you?

No, you see, very soon they had parades out there. Yeah. And after carnival, we'd have them floats for carnival, well, they hadn't much news for parades. Sometimes we'd have a little parade. Well, I played a couple of parades, alright, but, like for the old fellas, they may give something, we have a parade. I played a couple of their parades on the land.
Did they ever use any music for funerals there too, when they buried their members of the ensemble?

Let's see. I just could remember they had two funerals. A boy by the name of Henry Jewel, where his daddy used to play bass in the brass band. And I know a young fella, me and him come up together, because he used to stay down there by the name of Joe Camo. He was pretty good trombone, he was playing trombone. Well, when he died, they brought us a boy out in the country, well, we made up a little brand and played in suits. That's about the only one that went out, all our equipment.
When you came to New Orleans, did you find there was much difference in the music between this and the country bands? Much different. It was very different? Much different. What way was it?

Well, the boys here, they had more of a jazz swing. Yeah. We didn't call it Dixieland then, they used to call it jazz. Yeah. And when I was in Tibidale, well, I had them old fellas like Joe Oliver, Freddie Kepler, all them old trumpet players. Well, they used to call it ragtime. Yeah.
Did you ever hear them out in the country? Did they ever go up there?
They used to come out in the country, Frankie Duesen.
They'd come up there that way.

Yeah, that's what got me stuck on the trombone by looking at Frankie Duesen. I was a little kid, but I used to like that. You liked that? I'd stare in under the band from the time to get there till the time to leave.
He was a pretty good trombonist, Frankie Duesen?
Frankie Duesen, yeah, in them times.
Yeah.

Yeah. It was much different than playing trombone line in them times when I was coming up. Yeah. See, now you sing in the country. You just say, that's what they say, you play in lead all the time. Yeah.
What did they do then? You mentioned that the way you used to vamp. Did Duesen do that way or how did he?

Yeah, he used to play, you didn't play Red Whitney, call that player. You would look like you was a, you just play all for him. Because your music was written that way. It wasn't, sometimes you catch a portion in there as a soloist like, but then it dropped back, you know, while you playing all for him with a different melody all together. Did you say like a harmony part?
Yeah.
That's right.
Is it more like a melody you say at some time or was it more like a bass part or? Sometimes you catch some vamp in there.
But it always was a melody man. Yeah.
But not the same melody that the lead was? No. Sort of make another little tune around that, around that tune.
Yeah, but it's, I think. I liked it.

I used to like it. Well I forgot to ask if you started on the slide or the valve trombone. Oh I started on the slide. The slide, right on the slide. Yeah. Frankie Duesen, was he playing slide when you first heard him?
No, he was playing valve. He was playing valve. Mm-hmm, that's where he played too. Later on he started with that slide.
Yeah. You like the slide better than the valve?

The slide is much better but I, a valve is more basic I can tell you that. Well you could jump the fence, you'd plenty on the slide. Yeah, you could slide it right on the slide. Yeah, you could slide it right on the slide. Yeah, you could slide it right on the slide. Yeah.
But a valve had to come true. Yeah, that's the exact note on that.

Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's was wonderful times then. When I first came down here we used to, when I did start to go in Goodwill, things were pretty good. That's in the 20s, early 20s. Well in 26 I was playing with Chris Keller.
Well can you tell us a little bit, before you get there about your lessons with Dave Perkins, what he taught you, what kind of a book you used or anything else you can remember about your lessons?

Well he didn't give me no book, he just, he written me out scales. I learned them and what the hardest part about it was to them, that time, I had to keep time like, . Yeah, slide the grip to the door and bring it up on the board. Yeah, that's indeed. He's, instead of me, he's watching my notes and saying I'll be watching my feet trying to get that together. Yeah. Well he, he gave me a pretty good eye there on me, but I didn't finish too much on him because I wasn't able, because he was charging a dollar a lesson. How often did you go? Every week or more often? He was, you have to take about two lessons a week all right, if not he wasn't fooled with you.
Yeah. That'd be expensive then, but a dollar less than that.
Enough time, I'm telling you. A dollar less than that.
Did he have a method book to teach you out of? He said he didn't have a regular method book.
No.
Did he, did he have some kind of a, a music for you to hear? Oh yeah.
He just wrote out the things in part of him. Yeah. Um, how much did you practice? You were working then I guess in the daytime too? Did you have another job when you first came?
Oh yeah, I was, when I first came down here I was working.
Did you have much time to practice or? Well. Did you join a band right away?

Yeah, I got in the first. Little band was recent. What's the name of that? I'm telling you the truth, the first band I played in, little fellow on the corner by the name of son Wilson. What did you ever do? We played at Advertise. And that night I'll never forget, we played back there on Contise Street. And the boy, we cooked up son, he was, he was there with the, he was on the drum. And lucky he brought a kazoo. A few bands that could still come telling you, man it'll been something.
Okay, why that doesn't play like that?

No, and I couldn't do too much on the drum board, I'm telling you it was pitiful. And another band I played with was, uh, uh, did you see what was the name of this young? I forget his name, but Ross, he was one-eyed fellow. He played way up from a place called Cherokee Man. I think he was on the label this night. I know he was a holler at night. He was playing up. He couldn't play up with one piece after the bucket got a hold of it. And when I, da He played that a fellow way over a couple of doors from there. Why don't you tell that one-eyed nigga to knock the bottom out the bucket of the beak.
That's not a head of it.

See, every time he come up with the bucket had a hold of it. Yeah, well I'm telling you, I had to come up the hard way and had some tough reps. Finally, well, uh, started playing with a pretty good band. They called it the Liberty Bell. Liberty Bell.
I've heard of it. I don't remember who was in it, but who else was in it?
Yeah, there was a boy walking around here. No, he's blind. He'd been blind every time. He used to call him Brown, uh, Frey. He was playing Frey.
Yeah, he used to play harmonica and then clarinet.

He was playing clarinet. He still plays harmonica. Oh, he used to play too. Boy on bass, we called him T-boy. Little fella by the name of Freddie, he was playing carnet. And a little bit of short fella, about that high, called him Dad. He was playing Bouncy. Oh yeah, he just died, I think, last year.
Yeah, I didn't know he was dead. Yeah, yeah, he died.
Little dad, yeah. Well, he used to play, uh, banjo. Used to have six string banjos there.
Oh yeah, tune like a guitar.
Yeah, that's right. Did I tell you, did I call the drummer name? Well, it seemed like you did.
No, I didn't, but I forget it.
He was a little fella from uptown. He was playing, uh, playing, uh, drum. And after that, well, I come down this way.
Oh, speaking of drummers, I'm still thinking about this fella called Cookshop Son. Did you ever know his real name?
No.

Professor Minetta told us about him too. He used to play with him, um, with, uh, Bob Lyons in a little, uh, marching band they had. Yeah. Talked about him. And every time Huey Long would come to town, they'd get out that band. He liked Bob Lyons. And they'd meet him at the station, march him over to the Roosevelt Hotel.
Mm-hmm. Cookshop Son.
And he always got Cookshop Son. He told about the little shop they had.
Mm-hmm.
That his mother had, I guess, up there. That's right. But you never did know his real name?
No.
I don't think Jesse did.
His stepdaddy was named Jesse. Who was that his? His stepdaddy. His stepdaddy. Yeah, he was named Jesse. Jesse.
Was he a musician?
Yeah, he used to play ghetto. He used to play with, uh, his, uh, His band was named the Silver Leaf.
Oh, yeah. Jesse.
What did he play again?
Ghetto.
I think he was a chessie. Mm-hmm. Six-string band, or rather, well, I'd say a guitar. Yeah. His name was Jesse.
Um, is there anything else about Cookshop Son you can remember? That he, that he mostly, uh, in parade, I don't remember if he played bass drum or snare drum.
Well, he playing bass drum, yes. Is he still, uh,
Is he still alive? Yeah.

Is he still around? Yeah. If it's the same cook, cause that's the only cookshop son I know. That's what we used to call him. I didn't know he was still living. Did you mean happy? No, I don't think it would be happy.
It wouldn't be happy ghost and... Yeah, cause he, I know he's, he's still playing. Black happy, he plays in the Eureka. Yeah.
Wasn't red happy? It was a red happy.

Well, he used to play with, uh, Bob and I. Yeah, he played with Joe Oliver. I know some people say, he was an Ory, I think for a while. Yeah, he's one of the more times than me. You were supposed to be our best drummer we had, yeah. I've heard that he was very good, yeah.
Yeah. I think he stayed, Ory. Oh yeah, he been dead long ago. Mm.
Mm-hmm. That stuff
He was supposed to be our best drummer we had.
I've heard that he was very good.
Yeah.
I think he's dead.
Oh, yeah. He's been dead long ago.
That's the only cook shop son I know. I never didn't know his real name or anything about him. If he's still living or what happened?
Let's see. Cook shop. I think I'm kind of mixed up on that. Cook shop son is the one I was trying to have that kazoo.
Yeah, you mentioned him. Yeah, you mentioned him. I had him mixed up with what I'm telling you, but we usually call him Fu Klo.

Fu Klo? Yeah, Sun. There's Fu Klo that's still playing. Robert Lewis, is that his name, plays bass drum. Sun Fu Klo. Yeah, he's still playing. There's another one they call Sun on the drums. So Fu Klo was kind of tall.
Kind of tall, yeah. He is playing drums. Yeah, he's playing in the Eureka band.

Eureka band. I seen him in the Connors because I oughta ever grow up there. Either of me be playing a parade. Yeah, I was mixed up. Cookshop, I mean, Cookshop Sun is the one I was telling you about. He had the kazoo. He had the kazoo. That's the first job I went on. He played dance work then too.
He had a whole drum set playing.
The drum set in that kazooke in his mouth. If we wouldn't have been there, it would have been Peter.
What kind of trombone were you playing then? Was that the con that you were playing then? Yeah. You bought it here in town?
Yeah, I bought it from Shiki Con. Oh yeah. I bought a good horn soon as I came.
Silver horn? Yeah, silver.
I think in them time it cost me sixty some dollars. That would put a good horn in them days.
I heard in the old days they used a smaller bell. Now they like big bells. Six inch.
Six inch bell.
That would be the small one?
Yeah.
Would you like the small bell bigger or the smaller? Which is better?

I mean would you like the little one? I think, with my experience, about a seven inch ought to be. That ought to be a little bit better. It gives you a heavier tone. About seven. Yeah. That's about the best of all I was playing. I know that's what I would use. Because I knew that I know it's when they're all in the drum.
About seventh

We get jobs in there in the week. We play them. Not gonna get a job any day. Pay more than my job for waking or I'll stop and go play that job. Some little job, like you used to call them bonquets. It didn't play but uh two dollars but I don't care why I was waking. I was not going to go play that bonquets for the partner you have. So, oh man them dinners. Oh yeah, lots to eat. Oh yeah, you had plenty of fun. You had nothing strong but you had this uh what you called it nail beer. Nail beer?
Nail, nail. Not no nail. Oh yeah, during prohibition yeah. Yeah. Something like two-thirds of one percent.
Mm-hmm, all like that. Something like we did. I don't know. I'm telling you, we used to have the time.
Would you play out in the open at those bonquets?

No, we used to be in the hall. Oh, the hall. Yeah. All everyone operated was in the hall. Like a dance hall. Yeah, like the cooperators, perseverance, new hall, sometimes the economy. That's what he, that's them old societies. Yeah. That's what they called the anniversary. They called them bonquets.
Every year they'd have them the same day ten of them. That's right. That's right.
Well then you'd, would you play and then eat later or, or, or do you?
So they'll usually stop at 12 o'clock. Yeah. As soon as you get there, before you hit a tune, you could go get your dinner.
That's at 12 o'clock noon? Yeah.

Yeah. Go ahead and then get your gumbo and your chicken stew. Chicken gumbo and chicken stew. And pardon to use the feet. That is good. Mm-hmm. Then you go up and you play. You might play, um, or you get another little snack of one and you refresh it. It's really good. You play till five o'clock. I had to get two dollars for it. And I don't care why I was waking. When they had one of them, I was waking. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah, I quit and go to that tunnel.
I was going to ask some more about that band I mentioned before that you played in the Piku. Oh. And the Milton, Mr. Milton was telling us about just two days ago.
Well, that was, that was the last band I'm playing. Yeah, Piku, you had a piece there, uh, it's called Get Busy Right. stuff 된 된
된
된 된 된 된 된 된 된
That is at the very end? The little chop is all by itself? The trombone bar?
Yeah. That's what he heard. It didn't have been so long. It just didn't look like I forgot the air and everything. Then my mind ain't all so far enough. You know I just lose my wife.
Yes, I remember I was at the wake.
Oh, that's right. You see you at the wake. About two or three weeks ago? Yeah, on Blandin's. At Blandin's. Yeah, it was Easter Saturday. I mean Good Friday.
Good Friday. Right over there at Sheik. We just saw Sheik walking over there by the corner here a minute ago.
Yeah. If he knew you were coming there, he already came with you.

He was on the way to George Gano. He said he had to be there. He was the one to take him some papers and try some numbers with him. So he was in a hurry to run over. He would have stopped there.
